answers.flag: Option D also meets the requirement if Evaluate Target Health is set on the primary alias to the weighted records (a nested failover-over-weighted design), so only the LEAST-overhead cue separates A from D, and the key depends on the zero-weight record being returned when every nonzero-weight record is unhealthy.

case.label: D
case.text: A failover alias record whose primary is the weighted records and whose secondary is the S3 website is a documented, working pattern: with Evaluate Target Health on the primary alias, Route 53 treats the primary as unhealthy when all three weighted records fail their health checks and answers with the S3 website alias. It does not rely on the less-known rule that a weight-0 record is returned only when all nonzero-weight records are unhealthy, so a careful candidate could prefer it as the more explicit design. It costs a rename and extra records, but the stem never says how much overhead those add, and D does not state Evaluate Target Health, so the stem gives no way to rule it out except by the overhead wording alone.

case.label: B
case.text: A scheduled script that repoints the record when the us-east-1 load balancer fails would also move users to us-west-2, and it uses the same ELB health checks for instance replacement. It is defensible only if one ignores the LEAST operational overhead constraint: the script must be written, scheduled and maintained, and failover waits for the schedule, whereas failover alias records do this natively. The stem makes the overhead constraint explicit, so B loses on the stated constraint, not on correctness.

answers.flag: Option B (a CNAME to the load balancer DNS name) also stops the intermittent errors because it follows the ALB's changing addresses; the stem separates it from D only through the MOST cost-effective cue and the 'millions of DNS queries' hint, so the key depends on alias queries to AWS resources being free while CNAME queries are billed.

case.label: B
case.text: app.example.com is not the zone apex, so a CNAME is allowed there. A CNAME to the DNS name AWS assigned to the Application Load Balancer always resolves to the current addresses, which removes the stale-IP cause of the errors with no code and no maintenance. The query-charge difference between a CNAME and an alias to millions of queries per month is small in dollars, so a careful candidate could call B equally cost-effective; the stem never says the name is at the apex, never states a budget, and does not say that alias is needed for health evaluation.
